13013:
The TOSEC standard Adam linked to is definitely more detailed than the one I read before. I note that they simply use a hyphen in parentheses for an unknown publisher, whereas I've been using something like "(unknown author)". I believe Adam correctly described how to use the [h] flag for programs hacked by someone else, which seems to apply to a wide variety of circumstances. For Richard's modification of Chicken to run in MESS, you could probably also use the [f] flag -- "The original software has been deliberately hacked/altered in some way to 'improve' or fix the image to work in a non-standard way, e.g. 'fixing' a software that is supposed to run in PAL to run on a NTSC system."

I will take these updated guidelines into account when naming software in the future. Of course, there are many programs already on-line or on the FTP server which could also be changed. Most (but not all) programs with multiple authors given are a hack rather than a true collaboration. I probably won't update these names in the near future.

Paul

I think I understand it now.

(copied for clarity)
VSR (Voice Status Register) Format:

+-----+--------+-----+--------+-----+--------+-------+------+
| INC | TONE A | INC | TONE B | INC | TONE C | VIBRA | VOLN |
+-----+--------+-----+--------+-----+--------+-------+------+

In 'NOTE' order

VOLume Noise, Auto incrementing.
VIBRAto, Auto incrementing.
TONE C, load.
INC PC, after tone C load.
TONE B, load.
INC PC, after tone B load.
TONE A, load.
INC PC, after tone A load.

So, by playing with the VSR you can make NOTE1 do:

NOTE1: Duration,C
NOTE1: Duration,B
NOTE1: Duration,A
NOTE1: Duration,CB
NOTE1: Duration,BA
NOTE1: Duration,CA
NOTE1: Duration,CBA

Wow that's flexible.

I am once again amazed by the ingenuity of the Bally/DNA developers.

It's always a pleasant surprise to come across an unarchived tape program from a well known company. Of course, it's best when you can actually figure out how to use said program. In this case, the program in question is Music Compiler from Perkins Engineering. The first mention of this program is in Arcadian volume 2, issue 10, page 97, in  which Perkins Engineering describes upcoming software for use with the Blue Ram expansion:

"Then we will provide the software necessary to have the Blue Ram act as a compiler for music programs. Using Processor Technology format, one can simply enter musical selections and the software will convert that into the proper language that the Bally can understand."

The next mention comes in Arcadian volume 3, issue 2, page 18. The news here talks about John Perkins giving a demonstration of the Blue Ram to a computer club:

"Next, we listened with pleasure to several Bally compiled musical selections from Bach and Handel in three part harmony. It was explained that the compiler is used to translate a person's own composition or regular sheet music into a form that is played by the Bally."

And that's actually the last I can find. The fact that it's never actually advertised makes me think that it was never released, although it clearly got to a point where it was usable.

I found the main Music Compiler program on a tape in Ken Lill's collection. It's a reasonably long program saved in 300 baud. The opposite side of the tape was labeled as Sarabande, and has a pretty short bit of machine data to load into memory. I assume this is the data to be compiled. Handel composed a song named Sarabande, so this fits with the newsletter. I unfortunately don't see any other songs.

The programs seemed to process OK. Sarabande is a little strange because there were actually two sections on the tape, the second one much shorter and lower volume. The first section ends with U&
(64)=0. The second has a few bytes not seen in the first section, then U&(64)=0 again, then a STOP TAPE message followed by :RETURN; RUN. My best guess was that the extra bytes and U&(64)=0 in the second part should be removed, but I've made a version both doing this and leaving everything alone.

I don't have any instructions for the program. My best guess was to input the Music Compiler program, then input the song data, then run the program. Music Compiler ends with simply :RETURN, while the song ends with :RETURN; RUN, so that fits. I'm actually not even certain whether to run it in Bally BASIC or Blue Ram BASIC. There aren't any expanded BASIC keywords in the program. But I've tried it both ways, with both versions of Sarabande, and nothing works. Using the unedited Sarabande always made BASIC reset. Using the edited version, Music Compiler did at least run, but nothing played. In Bally BASIC, it printed out a question mark. In Blue Ram BASIC, it printed out the message "NO COMPRENDE:" from line 80 of the program.

I'll go ahead and include the code at the end of this message, and upload the files I have to the group. If anyone can figure out how to use it, or has ideas for me to test, let us know.

Paul

13055:
Thanks for pointing out the composite schematic, Ken!

Please pay no attention to the table of contents that I made for that group of articles that Ken pointed out.  I just noticed that the TOC doesn't make sense to me anymore, so it certainly won't make sense to someone else.  I do recall posting that as a work in progress and then never getting back to it.  The composite schematic originates from:

Sandin, Dan. "Direct Video Circuit Diagram." ARCADIAN 2.4 (Feb. 25, 1980): 28. Print.

A link to the issue that the schematic appears in is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_2/arcadian_vol_02_issue_04.pdf

Ken points out that there is no need for the BNC connector, which is more typical of being needed for the input that would perhaps be found on a monitor back in the late 1970's.  Since the schematic is by Dan Sandin I should point out that the Bally Arcade unit that he modified may have been used in a lab at University of Illinois at Chicago.  Sandin was involved in early graphics work as this university.  Dan was a mover and shaker in the computer art computer in the '70's and '80's.  Here is an example from of his "Circle Graphics Habitat" which is attributed (by pen in the upper-left corner of the scan) to Ted Nelson's 1974's "Computer Lib" book.  Here's a link to the article about the "Circle Graphics Habitat:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass-uv-1_articles/The_Circle_Graphics_Habitat.pdf

Here is a link to more information about "Computer Lib:"

After you get those controllers working well a quick spray of contact cleaner will do wonders for the paddle.  I've "saved" many Atari paddles this way and it works just as well on the Astrocade joysticks.  The brand I use is Techspray Ecoline Contact Cleaner, but your local electronics dealer should have something that works fine.  Just avoid WD-40 at all costs!

>>
When I got the system it came with half a dozen different cartridges so I'll have something to start off with.
>>

Great!  Maybe you have some that I mentioned already, as they are the most common.  If you do want the AstroBASIC send me an email.

>>
The details on the mod for the composite video looked easy enough to perform and I should have all the parts on hand for that.
>>

Let us know how it goes.  I suppose a composite upgrade wouldn't be worth it if you couldn't get color, so hopefully you can get that to work.

>>
Does anyone happen to have pictures of the insides of a cartridge?
>>

I see that Lance already pointed out the protoype carts PCBs, but those certainly are not what you'll typically find.  Here are clear pictures of the solder and component sides of the Astrocade PCB:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Astrocade%20BASIC%20PCB/AstroBASIC%20Cart%20PCB.html

While you won't a 300-Baud interface for AstroBASIC (it has a built-in 2000-Baud interface), it's still an interesting piece of hardware.  Here is are pictures of the 300-Baud interface, inside and out:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/audio_interface/audio_interface.html

Here are pictures of another nice piece of kit: the Lil' White 32K RAM expansion:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Lil_White_RAM/Lil-White-Ram.html

A few people (including myself) have made EPROM boards before.  The bottom of this page has some pictures of a couple of them:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/hardware_pictures.html

I thought that there were pictures of regular cart PCBs online, but if I guess that I never got around to making any.  I suppose I'll do that one day in the future.

>>
Are there any cartridges that are not that good (with plenty available) that could be used as a donor cart for the case and PCB?
>>

1) Common Not-Even-Games Carts: "Biorythm" and "Elementary Math & Bingo"
2) Common Not-So-Much-Fun Game Carts: "Star Battle"
3) VERY Common Fun Games: "The Incredible Wizard" and "Tornado Baseball/Tennis/Handball/Hockey"

Out of those carts you should be able to find a few for five bucks or less.

>>
It may be cool to remove the ROM, cut an opening in the cartridge case, and add a socket in place of the chip so an EPROM emulator could be plugged into it.  That would make it easy to download and try out new programs.
>>

Yes, this works.  Or you could buy GaMBITS Ulti-Multi Cartridge.  Ken Lill mames these.  I'm not sure if he has any now, but he seems to make a small batch about once a year.  Here's a link to pictures of all the multicarts that have been made for the Astrocade (only the GaMBITS mulicart is available anymore):

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Multicarts%29/Carts_%28Multicarts%29.html

Here's the documentation for the "Ulti-Multi Cartridge" including a list of games (each new cart run usually has very slight on what is contained on the cart):

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/multicarts/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29.html

Finally, there is the 512K MaxFlash prototype cart.  Only about five of these were made, and it never left prototype stage.  You can program the cart via USB (although you do need the original MaxFlash Programmer for the Atari 8-bit (which is easily obtainable by anyone, now).  There was no reason (other than lack of funds) for this prototype not have been produced.  That cart is more for development of one large game though.  The cart can NOT hold individual ROMs larger than 4K in one bank.  It is bankswitched and thus you could potentially have one 512K program that uses all 128 banks.  The first 4K would not move and then you'd be able to switch the second back in and out of the other 127 banks.  For more on this prototype cart, check this out:

http://www.bally128k.com/maxflash/maxflash.htm

The cartridge programmer is available here (yes, the Bally version uses the exact same one as the Atari 8-Bit version does-- they were designed by the same person):

http://www.atarimax.com/flashcart/documentation/

Good luck getting your Astrocade up and running!

Adam

Nobody from Bally, Dave Nutting or Astrovision/Astrocade has confirmed or denied this, but I believe this cart was actually started by Bally as PacMan. They had the coin-op rights.

Atari made the first ever 'Home Rights' licence and quickly produced the PacMan cart to head off Bally. Suing Magnavox over KC Munchkin helped convince Bally to sit on the cart.

Astrovision/Astrocade after buying the system knew 'Munchie' (as they coulden't get the PacMan name) would be a system seller, went to court to try to get Atari to let them sell it.

It was later released by a third party (Esoterica?) in a limited run as Muncher.

How it got from Astrocade to Esoterica is still a mystery also.

13085:
How could you say Muncher was supposed to be Munchie and not Pac Man.
Everything except the controls (where you don't move automatically in

Bally/Midway was Namco's US Arcade releasing partner, and they assumed

programming it, until Atari made a deal with Namco directly for the
home rights.   Which left Bally with a home version of Pac-Man they
couldn't call Pac-Man.   Same with Bally/Midway being Taito's US
arcade releasing partner for Space Invaders, and then Atari went over
Bally's head and went to Taito directly.  Remember Gun Fight was a
Taito game in the arcade and Bally brought it home.

As most of you know, ever since the new Yahoo Group interface (Neo) came out, it has made it difficult to read messages online (it's more like reading ads).  Receiving messages to your email account and posting from your email address makes using the group MUCH easier.

If you want to read past messages then reading them online now is also made more difficult by the Neo interface.  Is you use some version of Windows, then I advise you to download past messages (there are about 13,000 of them) using PGOffline Reader:

http://www.personalgroupware.comm

I've been using PGOffline for many years now and I love it.  The current version of PGOffline is in beta again, as the Neo interface changed whatever rules that PGOffline was using to download messages and it stopped working.  Apparently Yahoo doesn't share the information on how messages are downloads, so it needed to be figured out before PGOffline could be fixed.  Still, beta or not, I'm able to read past messages using PGOffline without a hitch.

Yahoo limits the amount of messages that you can download to about 2,000 a day, and then it locks your account for some (as far as I can tell) non-specific amount of time (I'm not sure how long)-- not longer than ABOUT half a day it seems.  I can usually download 2,000 in the morning and then another 2,000 in the evening.  While your account is locked you won't be able to post any messages on Yahoo Groups using any method, nor will you be able to read any messages if the group requires you to log-in to do so (BallyAlley does not require this).  You can avoid this situation by setting PGOffline to download some number less than 2,000 at a time.  Maybe try downloading 1,800 or 1,700 messages at a go.

It took me about four days to download all the messages on the BallyAlley group while downloading in both the morning and late evening.  It's worth the time!

In message 2481 (February 6, 2006), Adam wrote:
>>
One of these days I need to emulate the C64 again, if for nothing else then to play my
favorite version of Activision's Beamrider
>>

I wrote this eight years ago.  Why am I bringing up this old posting?  Well, I STILL play Beamrider and my friend mentioned recently that Jay Fenton programmed it.  Surely that couldn't be true.  Well it is true.  I even posted in the Yahoo Group that Jay programmed the game.  However, it was mostly a cut and paste posting and somehow I overlooked the C64 conversion of Beamrider.

It's interesting that Jay programmed this game in 1985, as this was right after he'd been working with the Z80 CPU for so long (on the Astrocade and then with the Z80 for the arcade games).  Then Jay went on to program for the 6502 on the C64.  I wonder what he thought of that CPU in comparison?  Then Jay went on to program for the Mac, so he was then using Motorola's 68000 CPU series (or maybe by then he was using a high-level language).

Here is a link on about the Beamrider game:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beamrider

Here is a link about the C64 version of Beamrider on a UK site:

http://www.lemon64.com/?mainurl=http%3A//www.lemon64.com/games/details.php%3FID%3D251

Here is a link to the box cover (front and back) of the game:

http://atariage.com/box_page.html?SoftwareLabelID=23

Here is a scan of the 2600 manual of the game (it is basically the same as the one I remember on the C64):

http://atariage.com/manual_thumbs.html?SoftwareLabelID=23

Here is an overview video of the game on YouTube:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4efaxSR-yvs

What's weird is that -I've- never written a review of this game.  I've mentioned it in passing SO many time, and yet I've never say down and written a proper review.

If the Astrocade had caught on (but it didn't) and then a hi-res version of the unit had been released (well, again, none came out) then I can well imagine that Jay would have written Beamrider for this little system.  Can you imagine if the Astrocade had support from Activision?

Oh, and for fun, here is a short review of Beamrider that my four-year old son wrote in 1998 (!):

http://www.orphanedgames.com/ocgs/issue8/dominic.html#Beamrider

Give the game a try someday-- it's available on SO many systems that I'm
 sure it must be available on SOME classic system that you enjoy!

Adam

13128:
Here is where you'll find pics of the UltiMulti Multicart.  It's the older version, but it should look about the same:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Multicarts%29/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29.html

Here is the documentation for the older version of the multicart.  The new version should be about the same:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/multicarts/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29.html

When "Crazy Climber" and "War" were for sale, each of those carts were $50 each.  Michael Garber granted permission to put those two games onto the multicart, so it's like getting his two games plus all these additional ones for free.  How can you lose?

The multicart contains all of the Astrocade released cartridge library and most of its prototypes plus many of other interesting bits.  The carts that were released by Bally and Astrocade don't require extra RAM, but a handful of carts by third-party publishers did require it (Blue Ram BASIC, for example).  Some games that were originally only released on tape have been modified to run as cartridges, and some of these "BASICarts" require extra RAM as well to work (even if the original game didn't need it).

The program listing for the last version of GaMBITS UltiMuli multicart is color-coded.  Programs that require extra RAM are highlighted in purple.  You can see the listing here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/multicarts/multicart_%28GaMBITS%29/UltiMulti_Version_1_5_1.pdf

Most people don't have extra RAM... so they won't be able to take advantage of these extra games.  That's okay.  Think of all the other games that you WILL be able to play.

As a user of the cartridge myself, I can attest that I don't really use any carts in my collection anymore except for AstroBASIC (which has the built-in tape interface).  I just leave the multicart plugged into my unit and change the settings so that I can play whichever game suits my fancy at the time.

If you don't have the UltiMulti already, then I highly recommend it.  If you have it already, then I advise you do get the new version.  I'll be sending Ken my multicart in the next few days and I look forward to the upgrade.

Adam

13140:
That's correct Bill, you'll send me your console for modification.  The mod will be almost identical to the custom mod I did on my Astrocade console years back, with the exception of using a composite cable instead of an S-VIDEO cable.  You can view my original mod here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/s-video_mod/mike_di_salvo_pics/mike_di_salvo_pics.html

I decided to use composite for a number of reasons, most important was for compatibility.  Many newer TVs and AV receivers have dropped the S-VIDEO connection, but still have composite (my new VIZIO 70" for instance).  The picture should be almost as good as S-VIDEO, and certainly better than RF.  You'll also have RCA for audio (L/R) mono, just like the original modification. 

There are no holes drilled in the console, no permanent modification to the motherboard etc.  I've never been big on driller holes in consoles, let alone vintage ones.  You can return the console to 100% original at any time.  The RF cable and modulator will be mailed back with your console. 

I'm choosing to do the mod instead of offering the kit for a number of reasons, most importantly to insure compatibility: we've got 30+ year old consoles, multiple motherboard revisions and BIOS etc.  I want to make sure what I install works, and works well for each user.  No shipping something back and forth multiple times. 

Also, I have an extreamly limited number of boards available and no plans to make more.  If the board doesn't work on your console, I can try another, etc.  If it just doesn't work for whatever reason, there is no charge.

I'll make a full announcement as soon as I have the cable I want to use and have them ordered.

13153:
From Craig Anderson:

I bought my Arcade in 1978 and immediately set out designing a chessboard, motion algorithms and legality checking in the hopes of incorporating some of the Spracklens' "Sargon" Z-80 program into it and making it a full-scale game. Unfortunately, I ran up against the memory wall at 2K and realized that Arcade Basic was not the way to go. Nutting Associates did ask me, in 1979 or 1980, if I would be interested in writing a Chess Cartridge for the Arcade and that's where the talk got started but I was way behind the curve as far as compilers, Forth, Z-80 assembler and down-on-the-metal repcard programming and I was intimidated by Scott Norris and Brett Bilbrey as far as skill went so the program never went anywhere. There was talk toward toward the end (Activision days) of Sargon itself becoming a reality in a possible deal with the Spracklens but that, like most Activision talk in the early 80s, turned out to be pickle-smoke as well. I sent the graphics to Fred Cornett and it was published in Cursor in the early 80s as simply a computer chessboard to be used between two players who were too broke to buy a chess set or to draw one on a piece of cardboard and collect enough toothpaste-tube caps to make their own. Fun times...

Craig Anderson

13172:
Actually, I'm not looking for game rights.  I am loking for the rights to make aNA strocade witht he same power, but a) cheaper, and b) networked.

The individual games I don't have to worry about because the games are second hand from original collections/ebay/thrift stroes/etc.  The reason why I don't need the rights to the individual games is because the networking system works independently of the game ROM.   Sort of like how the Galloob Game Genie for Genesis, which was authorized by Sega, changed games at the system level, so does my device add networking at the system level.   If one 2-or-more player game works with this system, then every game will.   No matter how great or obscure. It will work with everything from Gunfight and Checkmate to Blast Droids and any typed-in program.

Where it's coming from:  I've got a company who says they can research, build 2 prototypes, and draw mass building instructions for a small 5 figure fee or less.   I am currently preordering Net Genesises.   If I sell 1000 at $125 a piece, I can have enough money to get research, and build 1000 copies.  An AtGames Genesis cost $40 retail and included 40 Genesis Roms.  Since networking is a slightly tougher order.  I expect it to retail for about $100-125 to give myself enough cushion.  And I am not including any Genesis ROMs, (the ROMs being original cartridges or Sega authorized downloads), but you can use your original Genesis Cartridges, and if Sega likes my idea of advergaming, could offer free ROMs just for watching one commercial every time you first boot up a ROM, and only get a new commercial when you reset, change network opponents, change games, or power off and then restart.

The beautiful thing about this setup is every game will be networked, even if the rights are in limnbo.  We just won't show commercials until we negotiate the rights limbo.  So, if we had Nintendo systems, SNES and N64 Killer Instinct is a free game (assuming you have the original cartridge) with no commercials unless Nintendo and Microsoft come to some sort of agreement on these 2 titles.

Sprint Direct Connect is the Sprint walkie talkie system using cell phone frequencies.   The reason why Direct Connect is more desirable for my purposes compared to DSL or Cable is because of lightning-fast ping time.  If you took a ping measurement between Cleveland and Chicago, you get ping times of 40-75 ms.  But Cleveland and Chicago are 600 km apart.  Light travels at 300 km/ms.  So if data travels at the speed of light and takes the most direct path, you'd have 4 ms ping time.  A big difference between 40 and 4.    The reason why this is is because the network is designed to get you there, even if a city in the middle gets bombed.  The cost of that is a 50-200 milliseconds, which is within normal human reaction times.   So when you talk phone, if you are in the same room, you'll have the "Rita Repulsa effect."  (named so because the lips don't match the words on the phone.  Watch Mighty Morphin Power Rangers Year 1  and you'll see what I'm talking about.)  Most people wouldn't have anticipated video games that have unique controller inputs 60 times per second, pushing the optimal ping time to 16 ms.

So the computer needs are faster than the network.  Most people cured it before by mass trucking data in the Megabit range, and let the server be the ref and decide what happened and pass decrees and have the machines instantly rewind and fast forward.   That's why people pop out of your sights in a first person shooter before you pull the trigger.

Most machines can fit their controller data, random number data, and timestamp sync data under 33k.  The Astrocade uses 5 bits for north, south, east, west, and fire.   I don't know how many bits are in the analog controller.  Let's assume it's 8.  That's 13 bits/controller/frame.  Multiply that by 4 controllers and you have 52 bits/cycle.  Someone told me the Astrocade can have 60 controller cycles per second.   If that's the case then the total joystick data is about 3,000 bits/second, or 3 kb/s   Random numbers not tied to the timer need 8 bits/cycle.   But if the random number is a function of the timer, then all you need to do is make sure the timestamps sync, and the machine can handle random numbers based on the internal timer and a net ping signal to test for sync.

So Net traffic can fit comfortably under 33k both ways.   The only reason why Dreamcast failed is because the network had heavy ping.   They didn't have the bandwidth to compensate for poor ping.   But Sega was right when they say most games can fit under 56k.   The problem was ping time.   If you beat 16 ms two-way ping time, then you can have just a joystick stream.   No complicated computing of every piece of shrapnel (which Xbox bragged about in the Original Xbox days).

Enter Sprint Direct connect.  Once you establish a connection in 10-30 seconds, then you can privately transmit data in 1.1-1.5 ms/300 km, depending on network efficiency and traffic.  The traffic goes straight from your phone, from tower to tower in the shortest path possible, and connects in as close to a direct line as possible.  Since Sprint owns the whole connection throughout, there's no rights negotiations between parts of  networks resulting in weird reroutings.   It's basically a giant multi-mile LAN cable.    Now you can do a live joystick stream, and the result of that is that EVERY 2-or-more player game will work online, not just ones programmed for it.

The only weakness is distance.  If you're further than a half frame in ping time away, then you cannot do it.   But for a 60 frame/second game at 66% network efficiency, the range would be 1600 km.   You can find quite a bit more Astrocade friends over the Private Ultra Low Ping network than you would at a random stop to a classic game store, even though the range is 1600 km.    Would you travel 1600 km to find a cartridge of average value and rarity?   Now you don't have to to find Astrocade friends.

Finally I don't know if Warner Bros. owns the right to the Astrocade.   (The "Bally Astrocade" maybe in name only)  I just assumed it did.  So where would I go to have permission for these Net Astrocades built?

I have read the majority of the bankruptcy papers listed and there is no definitive answer to who currently gas rights to the arcade. There was a 5 year agreement between Astrovision and Bally. After the 5 years, supposedly the rights all reverted back to Bally since Astrocade and Nitron went "belly-up". Unless someone has a copy of the original agreement between Bally and Astrovision, this is all we can assume. There was a huge lawsuit frenzy put on by Atari against each of the "game" systems on the way that the data was stored and transmitted to the screen. They were winning every suit until Colecovision came along and the judge finally against them stating the US Monopoly laws.
Thie is all I know.

I received and dumped these carts recently. They were labeled "Bally Pin Demo" and "Space Invaders Demo". Despite the label, Bally Pin was identical to the released cart. 3) Final Test
4) Football

6) Ms Candyman and Sea Devil Multicart
7) Music Maker
8) Soccer (4 Different Pictures)
9) Solar Conqueror (7 different pictures)
10) Songs

All carts can be accessed from here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/cartridge_pics.html

Most of these carts were scanned by Paul Thacker.  The carts were on loan to him from Ken Lill's collection.  Ken Lill wrote some comments to me about a few of these cart on December 30, 2009:

"Each one of these was a prototype from either Dave Nutting Associates or the later software group Action Graphics, which was where most of the programmers were, including John Perkins. He was the one to give me these when he gave me rights to the Blue Ram, many moons ago.

"Solar has been misspelled, It is only called conquer, not Conqueror. Cosmic is also unfinished."

If you're into prototype carts, then today is really you're lucky day.  As for me, prototype carts have never been my thing... as long as a complete and finished version of the cartridge was released.

Enjoy!

13217:
I added two miscellaneous newsletters to BallyAlley.com:

1) Arcadian Local News (May 30, 1979) - This 4-page hand-written newsletter was written by Richard Belton and published by/for the Maryland Users Group. Among other topics, Richard discusses a phone call that he made to Bally Corp. asking about the memory add-on and keyboard expansion. Bally sent a letter to Richard, which he included in the newsletter.

2)  The Printed Circuit (January 1979) - Vol. 5, No. 1 (January 1979) - This 8-page newsletter was published by The Computer Hobbyists Group of North Texas. It doesn't seem to have anything about the Bally Arcade/Astrocade in it-- which doesn't mean it's not interesting to those interested in the Bally Arcade's history! From a handwritten note on the last page of this newsletter, I think that Bob Fabris had this in his collection because of the S-100 board specs that are presented in the newsletter. In the late 70's The Arcadian was tossing around the idea of making an S-100 bus upgrade available for the Bally, but nothing ever became of it in final form. Through personal letters from the Fabris Collection, it does appear that some work on it may have been begun, but I'm not sure how far it went.

These can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/misc_newsletters/misc_newsletters.html

I wasn't sure what to make of the Arcadian Local News.  Seeing it among the Fabris Collection was the first that I'd heard of it.  From its name I think it may have been meant to be a sub-set of the Arcadian... so I almost put it in the Arcadian area.  However, it's distinct enough that it stands on its own.  The "local news" was only sent to a handful of people (probably about ten of them), so this is rare and, like nearly everything I've come across in the Fabris Collection, is lucky to have survived all this time!

As for The Computer Hobbyists Group of North Texas newsletter, I couldn't find anything about this at all.  I seems that the user groups are fast becoming a forgotten piece of history!

Enjoy!

Adam

1) Connect Four (1980)(Robert Leake)(2000 baud).zip - Found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  It's a Cursor program.  The first few lines are machine language.

2) Connect Four Parameter Program (1980)(Robert Leake and Fred Cornett)(2000 baud).zip - Found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape hand-labeled "New Game COH".  It's a Cursor program.  It helps the user enter the machine language portion of the Connect Four code.


Overview:

Fred Cornett, the editor of Cursor thought very highly of "Connect Four."  The September 1980 issue of "Cursor" has two pages (52 and 53) that are notoriously difficult to read.  These pages the "Connect Four" LISTings.  The ink on the original pages used was light blue with orange bands running the length of the page.  This was done as a means of copy protection; it made photocopying the newsletter much more difficult.  That early form of program copy protection worked rather well, as the pages are hard-to-read even in the archived issue of Cursor on BallyAlley.com.


"Connect Four" Instructions from Cursor:

Editor's Note: This is the finest board game program we have ever seen written for the "Bally!"  The graphics, color and sound are excellent.
The computer makes each move totally cognizant of all the ramifications of his move.  Hence, you are forced to play very well indeed in order to win (it beats us 8 out of 10 times).  This program alone is well worth the $9.75 subscription price for "Cursor."

The object of this game is to get four of your playing pieces in a row (without any of your opponent's pieces in between) vertically, horizontally or diagonally before the computer or your human opponent does.

Pieces drop vertically in the selected column to the lowest unoccupied position.  To select a column, move the joystick left or right and squeeze trigger when indicator is over desired column. Joystick 1 always goes first.

This program loads in three separate segments; pay very close attention to the instructions, and input the information exactly as you see it.

Note: Starting with this issue, whenever 2 or more spaces are located together on a program line, C=SPACE. So, whenever you see "C", key in a space (this is done to make it easier for you to tell how many spaces are necessary).


Connect Four Parameter Program by Robert Leake - Adapted by Fred Cornett

This program MUST be input and run PRIOR to inputting the "Connect Four Main Body Program"!!!

After you have keyed this program into the computer and pressed "RUN", the screen will clear, and the following will appear:

This display is telling you to refer to the chart marked "LINE 2". Take the value shown in the box DIRECTLY below the "1" (which is 2), and input the value, check to see if you have input it correctly before pressing "GO"; the computer will space a line and print:

     LINE #2 2=

Check box 2 (which is 32), input value, hit "GO" and continue thusly. It must be stressed that you MUST check for errors before you press "GO" each time. If you make only one error, this program will not function properly!!

Line 1 (Title Line) is absolutely necessary for data in subsequent lines to be accessed (do not delete)!

After you have run the "Parameter Program", and input the data in lines 2 through 7, the next step is to delete lines 100 through 310. This can be accomplished in one of 2 different ways.

1. Lines 280 through 310 comprise a small program that will load lines 1 through 7 on tape. Merely follow the directions that will be printed, on your screen. Press "RECORD" on your tape machine and then press "GO" after the leader has cleared, the record head. Use :LIST and playback the tape to make sure it has recorded. (Lines 2 through 7, which prior to running the program, contained numbers in sequence, i.e., 12345678, etc., now contain garbage to include such things as "??A4#)/??&". Do not think you have done something wrong, the computer is merely trying to print info that does not conform to ASCII Code; you will see many on those lines.) If Lines 1 through 7 have loaded on tape, hit "RESET" and input tape, then key in "Connect Four Main Body Program".

OR

2. The only purpose of the "Parameter Program" is to assemble data in lines 1 through 7. Lines 100 through 310 are totally unnecessary after the data has been loaded. After you have completed inputting all the data for lines 2 through 7, you must delete all lines that follow Line 7. If you do this, do not bother to input lines 280 through 310 at the beginning (they only apply to loading lines 1 through 7 on tape). After you have deleted all lines except 1 through 7, key in "CONNECT FOUR MAIN BODY Program".

[The "Connect Four" program LISTings and data appear here in the newsletter.  Refer to the archived issue of Cursor (available on BallyAlley.com) to see them.]

After you have loaded the assembled lines 1-7 and the "Connect Four Main Body Program" into the computer, you must load String Arrays 77 through 84 with data.

This is done by typing in the following one line program without a line number:

FOR A=77T0 84;PRINT #1, "@(" ,A,")=",;INPUT ""@(A);NEXT A;RUN

Computer will print: @(77)=

Input the values from the following, checking for accuracy before pressing "GO":

STRING   VALUE    STRING   VALUE

 @(77) = 1200      @(78) = 100
 @(79) = 8         @(80) = 1
 @(81) = 12        @(82) = 150
 @(83) = 8000      @(84) = 0

If you have done everything correctly, the program will run perfectly. We have triple checked the info and listings for errors, there are none.

Next, we suggest you load the complete assembled program on tape; this will preclude any accidental loss of the program.

STEP 1: Load an unused tape into your tape recorder; press "PLAY" and run the tape a few feet past the end of the tape leader. Stop the recorder.

STEP 2: Load the following one line program into your computer without a line number- DO NOT PRESS "GO"!!

NT=1;CLEAR ; :PRINT ;TV=13:LIST ;F0R A=77T0 84;PRINT #1,"@(",A,")=",@(A),";",;NEXT A; PRINT ":RETURN ;RUN

NO NOT PRESS GO AT END OF PROGRAM LINE!!

STEP 3: Press "RECORD" on tape recorder;

Press "GO" on computer. Complete program including string arrays will load on tape.

HAVE FUN


That's the end of the docs from Cursor.  As you can see, getting this program up and running wasn't a simple matter at all!

Enjoy!

13235:
OK, here's the scoop from what I can tell.
If you take a picture of the Bally/ Astrocade on a CRT TV, you will get some of the picture as a large black line. This is due to it being interlaced and to the speed of the camera. If you were to use a newer TV (Especially a LED) you won't have that problem. The newer TV's are not interlaced but rather progressive scan. They start from the very top of the screen and go acrossto the right edge, then it shoots back during Horizontal Retrace to line #2. It is faster and smoother than Interlace.
Interlace jumps from line 1 to line 3 etc until all odd number lines are done and then it starts from line 2 and does all of the even lines.
Ken

13243:
I recently made contact with some engineers who worked on the Bally Astrocade and peripherals. Dick Ainsworth responded with a wonderful message and followed up with a request to join the Bally group! I hope the admins have a moment to verify his membership so that we can ask him questions about his experiences!
 

 "Hi Ian…
 

 I was glad to hear of your interest in the Bally system.  I wrote the Bally Basic programming book and created the easy entry keypad to go with it.  I also designed the music notation and programming system that used the keypad to compose music.
 

 The original Bally audio tape interface included a cassette with several of my programs in Bally Basic.  This audio cassette may have been the first distribution of computer software for the personal computer market.  In any event, while duplicating this cassette at GRT( Great Records and Tapes) studio I met Bill Gates who was duplicating the first cassette version of Microsoft Basic.  The recording contracts we had at that time had the phrase "your song or musical performance" crossed out and the word "your software program" inserted instead.  And so it began…
 

 I followed the Bally Basic programming book with several others, including the Color Computer Learning Lab.  My association with Bill led to my writing the manual for Microsoft Basic and my creation of the original Typing Tutor, published by Microsoft, IBM, Tandy, etc.
 

 I worked with Jay (now Jamie) Fenton and several other programmers at Dave Nutting Associates in designing some of the early Bally cartridges.  Specifically, I designed Bingo Math, the first educational software to use interactive programming and user-modeling techniques similar to coin-op games.
 

 I'd be glad to loan you some of the original work I wrote for Bally if you do not already have versions you can copy.
 

 My current software company lives at www.qwerty.com http://www.qwerty.com/.  
 

 Learning the finer points of BASIC with Bill Gates, Jamie Fenton, Tom DeFanti and others in those early days was a bit like learning to fly with Wilbur and Orville.  
 

 
 Regards…"

I followed the Bally Basic programming book with several others, including the Color Computer Learning Lab.  My association with Bill led to my writing the manual for Microsoft Basic and my creation of the original Typing Tutor, published by Microsoft, IBM, Tandy, etc.
I worked with Jay (now Jamie) Fenton and several other programmers at Dave Nutting Associates in designing some of the early Bally cartridges.  Specifically, I designed Bingo Math, the first educational software to use interactive programming and user-modeling techniques similar to coin-op games.
I'd be glad to loan you some of the original work I wrote for Bally if you do not already have versions you can copy.
My current software company lives at www.qwerty.com.
Learning the finer points of BASIC with Bill Gates, Jamie Fenton, Tom DeFanti and others in those early days was a bit like learning to fly with Wilbur and Orville.

Regards…"
